title: When was creation?
hookLine: what hour, what season was the world made? only the Creator knows (Japji 21)
tomorrow: what did Guru Nanak see when he looked up at the evening lamps?

lines: WHAT HOUR WAS THE WORLD MADE?
THE PANDITS, THE QAZIS, THE YOGI.
cards: At dinner a kid asks, out of nowhere: but when did the world start? What day? The adults at the table go quiet.
Guru Nanak asked the same question. In the Japji's twenty-first stanza: what was that time, what moment, what day, what season, what month, when the world took shape? Then he goes around the room.

The pandits didn't find the hour, or it would be written in the Puranas. The qazis didn't find it, or it would be written in the Quran. The yogi doesn't know the day, and nobody knows the season or the month.

teach.b: Then the answer: the Creator who made the creation, He alone knows.
Guru Nanak tells what came before in another hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Maru. For countless ages, he sings, there was only darkness. No earth, no sky.
No day, no night, no sun, no moon. Only the hukam, the divine order. Nobody there to keep a calendar.
So, in the Japji, the hour of creation belongs to the Creator, and the Japji says so out loud to the learned of every camp around it. It isn't a jab at anyone's books.

teach.h: A LINE AROUND WHAT BOOKS CAN HOLD.
teach.b: It's a line drawn around what any book can hold. And it isn't a shrug.
The stanza goes on to say that the Creator's greatness can't be described, and that anyone who claims to know it by himself won't be honored in the world to come.
Not knowing, in the Japji, is a kind of honesty, and a kind of praise.
Worth repeating at dinner: in a single stanza, Nanak names the scholars of the Puranas, the scholars of the Quran and the yogis, and gives none of them the date.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji each morning; its twenty-first stanza is read as a teaching of humility before what only the Creator, Karta Purakh, knows.

o: a festival marking the day the world began
a question the Japji says only God can answer
a date worked out by priests from old books

games.q: Japji 21, who knows the hour: tap the pairs.

s: the Japji gives the date of creation
it asks the hour and says only the Creator knows.
in a hymn in Raag Maru, Nanak sings of darkness before earth and sky
for countless ages only darkness, and only the hukam.
the Japji says one group of scholars did know the date
pandits, qazis and the yogi alike: none of them found the hour.

games.q: your little cousin asks when the world started, exactly, and you want to answer the way the Japji does. what fits?
o: nobody knows the hour; Guru Nanak says only the Creator knows.
the Japji says the yogis worked out the exact day and season.
it's written in one of the old books, if you look hard enough.
games.why: Japji 21: not the pandits, not the qazis, not the yogi; the Creator who made it alone knows.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one thing in your life you can't know yet: a result, a reply, an outcome. Don't solve it or rehearse it.
Let it sit there, unknown, while the breath comes and goes, and notice that you're still here with it.

wordCard.voice: When was creation? The Japji's question, and its answer: only the Creator knows.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji stanza 21: what was that time, what moment?

carryVoice: Hold this one gently: only the creator knows, and the not-knowing can be shared. Two of five from the Japji.
